passages.t: ‘Day and night I cry out before You’: a man near the Pit
passages.happening:
Psalm 88 has one of the longest headings in the Psalms. It reads, “A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah. For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite” (verse 1). Then the prayer: “O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You” (verse 1).

He asks God to listen (verse 2). Then he says how things are. “For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol” (verse 3). He feels already counted with the dead (verse 4). “I am forsaken among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom You remember no more” (verse 5).

He does not blame chance. He says God has done it. “You have laid me in the lowest Pit, in the darkest of the depths” (verse 6). “Your wrath weighs heavily upon me; all Your waves have submerged me” (verse 7).

And he is alone. “You have removed my friends from me; You have made me repulsive to them; I am confined and cannot escape” (verse 8). “My eyes grow dim with grief. I call to You daily, O LORD; I spread out my hands to You” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The heading names two sources: the sons of Korah, the temple singers, and Heman the Ezrahite. The book page notes this double heading. A Heman is named among David's chief musicians, with Asaph and Ethan (1 Chronicles 15:19). A Heman is also named among famous wise men, whom Solomon was wiser than (1 Kings 4:31). Whether these are one man is not known. ‘Mahalath Leannoth’ may be a tune, but no one knows for sure.

‘Sheol’, ‘the Pit’ and ‘the grave’ are all names for the place of the dead. The book page explains them in its part on Sheol. For an Israelite, death meant being cut off from the life of God's people, where God was praised.

Notice verse 8. In the ancient world, a person with a lasting illness could be kept apart from others. Friends might stay away, out of fear or shame. Whatever his trouble was, sickness or something else, this man has lost his people. The psalm never says what the trouble is. That may be part of why so many sufferers have found their own words in it.

Look at the first line again: ‘the God of my salvation’. He still calls God that. And he still cries ‘day and night’. That is not the same as feeling better. It is a man who keeps praying when nothing changes.
passages.later:
Job, too, cursed the day he was born (Job 3:3). Lamentations speaks of God who “has made me dwell in darkness like those dead for ages” (Lamentations 3:6).

Jesus knew what it is to be left alone. On the night he was arrested, “everyone deserted Him and fled” (Mark 14:50). In Gethsemane he said, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death” (Matthew 26:38).
passages.asks:
Psalm 88 does not ask you to feel anything. It gives words to someone who already feels this way, or who sits beside someone who does.

If your friends have drifted away in your trouble, notice that this man named it to God. You may tell God that you are lonely, and that it hurts.

passages.t: ‘Will Your wonders be known in the darkness?’
passages.happening:
Now the man argues with God, with six questions in three verses. “Do You work wonders for the dead? Do departed spirits rise up to praise You?” (verse 10). “Can Your loving devotion be proclaimed in the grave, Your faithfulness in Abaddon?” (verse 11). “Will Your wonders be known in the darkness, or Your righteousness in the land of oblivion?” (verse 12).

He does not wait for an answer. The questions just stand there.
passages.hearers:
These are not idle questions about the afterlife. They are an argument. The man is saying to God: if I die, I can no longer praise you among your people. Keep me alive, for your own name's sake.

Abaddon is another name for the place of the dead, from a word that means ‘to perish’. ‘The land of oblivion’ is the land of forgetting, where no one is remembered.

Many psalmists, as the book page says in its part on Sheol, did not yet know the full hope of life after death that comes later in the Bible. Isaiah would say, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). Psalm 88 prays from before that hope was spelled out. Its questions are honest about how dark death looked from where he stood.
passages.later:
Psalm 6 asks a question like these: “who can praise You from Sheol?” (Psalm 6:5). The book page's part on Sheol sets the lines side by side.

The New Testament speaks of a God who works wonders for the dead. Jesus wept at the grave of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35), and then called him out of it. Christians believe that the answer to verse 10 came at Easter. But that answer is not in Psalm 88, and these notes do not put it there.
passages.asks:
The man in Psalm 88 argues with God using God's own honour. You may do the same. Tell God why your life matters to his purposes. Tell him what you fear losing.

You do not need to answer his questions for him. Sometimes a question spoken to God is the most honest prayer there is.

passages.t: ‘Darkness is my closest companion’: a prayer that never turns
passages.happening:
He keeps praying. “But to You, O LORD, I cry for help; in the morning my prayer comes before You” (verse 13). Then: “Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?” (verse 14).

His trouble is old. “From my youth I was afflicted and near death. I have borne Your terrors; I am in despair” (verse 15). God's anger has swept over him like a flood. “All day long they engulf me like water; they enclose me on every side” (verse 17).

Then the last line. “You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion” (verse 18).

That is where the psalm ends. There is no turn to trust. There is no ‘But I will praise You’. The last word in Hebrew is ‘darkness’.
passages.hearers:
Most laments in the Psalms move from complaint toward trust. Psalm 13 does. Psalm 6 does. The book page calls Psalm 88 the one lament that never turns. It ends in the dark, and God kept it in the book anyway.

A first hearer would know that this psalm was sung. It has a heading for the choirmaster. That means God's people did not hide it away. They sang it together, at worship, perhaps for those among them who were in the dark.

What does it mean that this prayer is in the Bible? It means that God's people may pray even this. A believer may come to God with nothing but grief and questions and still be praying. The psalm does not make the darkness right. It shows that the darkness may be spoken to God.
passages.later:
Jesus prayed a psalm of darkness on the cross: “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34). Hebrews says that in his earthly life he “offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death” (Hebrews 5:7). Isaiah calls him “a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3).

When we cannot find words, Paul says, “the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26).
passages.hard:
Psalm 88 does not end with hope, and these notes will not give it a happier ending than the Bible gives it. If you are reading this psalm because it sounds like your life, it is not a sign that your faith has failed. The man who prayed it was still praying. That counts.

These notes do not give anyone's suffering a name or a diagnosis. But if darkness feels like your closest companion, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust today: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. Sorrow that lasts, or that takes away sleep, hope or the wish to go on, is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If someone you love prays like this, stay near them. Listen without hurrying them to the end of the psalm. And help them reach the people who can help.
passages.asks:
Can you let this psalm stand as it is? Many of us want to rush to a happy ending. Psalm 88 teaches patience with the dark, in our own lives and in the lives of others.

If you are in the dark now, you may pray these verses as your own, and the prayer still counts. If you are not, pray them for someone who is. And remember that Psalm 88 sits in a book of 150 psalms. It is not the whole book. But it is there, and it is true.
